content: Tubers are specialized plant structures that have undergone modification to store nutrients. These structures are enlarged and serve as a means for plants to survive through winter, regrow in the following growing season, and reproduce asexually. Tubers are classified into two main types: stem tubers and root tubers. Stem Tubers Stem tubers develop from thickened rhizomes or stolons. The upper or lateral parts of the tuber produce shoots that grow into stems and leaves, while the lower parts generate roots. These tubers typically form near the soil surface, often at the sides of the parent plant. Stem tubers are short-lived storage and regenerative organs that arise from shoots branching off a mature plant. New tubers, or offspring tubers, are either attached to the parent tuber or form at the end of a hypogeogenous rhizome. During the fall, the parent plant dies, leaving behind the new stem tubers, which contain a dominant bud. In spring, this bud regenerates into a new shoot, producing stems and leaves. By summer, the old tubers decay, and new tubers begin to form. Some plants produce smaller tubers or tubercles that function like seeds, giving rise to small plants resembling seedlings in morphology and size. While some stem tubers, such as those of tuberous begonias, are long-lived, many tuberous plants have tubers that only survive until the plant has fully developed its leaves. At this point, the tuber shrivels into a husk. Stem tubers often originate as enlargements of the hypocotyl section of a seedling, sometimes including the first node or two of the epicotyl and the upper section of the root. These tubers are typically vertically oriented, with one or a few vegetative buds at the top and fibrous roots emerging from the basal section. They usually have an oblong or rounded shape. Common examples of stem tubers include tuberous begonias and cyclamens. The mignonette vine (Anredera cordifolia) produces aerial stem tubers on tall vines, which fall to the ground and grow into new plants. Potatoes Potato tubers are specialized swollen stems that develop from enlarged stolons, which thicken into storage organs. These tubers retain all the structural features of a normal stem, including nodes and internodes. The nodes, also known as eyes, are arranged in a spiral pattern around the tuber, starting from the end opposite the stolon attachment point. Each node has a leaf scar, and the terminal bud forms at the farthest point from the stolon attachment, exhibiting apical dominance similar to a typical stem. Internally, potato tubers are filled with starch stored in enlarged parenchyma-like cells. They also contain the typical cellular structures of a stem, such as a pith, vascular zones, and a cortex. Potato tubers are produced within a single growing season and serve to perennialize the plant and facilitate propagation. In the fall, the above-ground parts of the plant die, while the tubers overwinter underground. In spring, the tubers regenerate new shoots, which utilize the stored nutrients to grow. As the main shoot develops, adventitious roots form at the base of the shoot near the tuber, and lateral buds on the shoot produce stolons. These stolons are elongated stems that grow during long days under the influence of auxins and high gibberellin levels, which inhibit root growth from the stolons. Before new tubers can form, the stolons must reach a certain age. The hormone lipoxygenase plays a role in regulating potato tuber development. When potato plants are grown from seed, stolons are easily recognizable as they emerge from the nodes near the soil surface. Tubers form close to the soil surface and sometimes even above ground. In cultivation, potato tubers are cut into pieces and planted deeper in the soil. Planting deeper allows for more space for tuber development, resulting in larger tubers. The planted pieces sprout shoots that grow to the surface, producing rhizome-like structures that generate short stolons underground. Once the shoots reach the soil surface, they produce roots and green shoots that grow into the mature plant. It is important to distinguish stem tubers, such as potatoes, from tuberous roots (or root tubers), such as sweet potatoes or dahlias. Root Tubers Root tubers, or tuberous roots, are modified lateral roots that have become enlarged to function as storage organs. While they differ in origin, they share similar functions and appearances with stem tubers. Notable examples of plants with root tubers include sweet potatoes, cassava, and dahlias. These structures enable plants to survive from one year to the next by acting as storage organs. Unlike true tubers, root tubers lack nodes, internodes, and reduced leaves. Instead, they exhibit the typical internal and external cellular structures of roots. Root tubers have a proximal end, which contains crown tissue that produces buds capable of growing into stems and foliage. The distal end typically produces unmodified roots. In true tubers, this arrangement is reversed, with the distal end producing stems. Root tubers are biennial in duration. During the first year, the parent plant produces the root tubers, and the plant dies in the fall. In the following year, the root tubers generate a new plant, consuming the stored nutrients to produce new roots, stems, and flowers. The remaining tissue dies as the plant forms new root tubers for the next year. Some plants, such as Hemerocallis fulva (daylilies) and their hybrids, develop large root tubers. H. fulva spreads through underground stolons that terminate in new fans, which grow roots that produce thick root tubers and send out additional stolons. Plants with root tubers are propagated by digging up the tubers in late summer to late winter, separating them, ensuring each piece contains crown tissue, and replanting them.
